USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The US should hold its current tariff posture and seek to engage China in high-level negotiations ahead of the planned Trump-Xi meeting at the G20 in Buenos Aires (scheduled for late November/early December 2018). No new escalatory steps should be taken before that meeting, but existing tariffs should remain in place as leverage. The $200 billion tranche at 10% should be kept as scheduled to rise to 25% on January 1, 2019, as a credible threat to incentivize Chinese concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.35 reflects a moderate but not existential threat to US interests. The trade war has imposed real costs: soybean prices are down 20% (Brookings), agricultural exporters and Midwest farmers are feeling pain, and US companies operating in China face collateral damage. The $250 billion in tariffs already in effect covers roughly half of US-China trade (Fox Business/Motley Fool), and China has retaliated on nearly all $130 billion of US exports to China. However, the overall macroeconomic hit to the US economy remains a 'minor blip' per Brookings analysis, and the US has structural leverage: China's export-dependent economy is more exposed to tariff disruption than the US domestic economy. The action score of -0.1 (hold) reflects the strategic calculus that the G20 meeting with Xi Jinping offers a near-term off-ramp. Escalating further before that meeting would undermine diplomatic prospects, while conceding now would squander leverage. The Washington Post reporting on 'crossed wires' shows that both sides have misread signals, with China feeling betrayed after previous deals were vetoed by Trump. This suggests the US should pursue clearer, high-level communication rather than additional unilateral tariff actions. The current posture — tariffs as leverage with a scheduled leaders' meeting — is the optimal position.
key_factors: $250 billion in US tariffs on Chinese goods already in effect, covering ~50% of bilateral trade
China has retaliated on nearly all $130 billion of US exports to China
Soybean prices down 20%, agricultural sector under significant pressure
Overall US economic impact described as 'minor blip' by Brookings
G20 Trump-Xi meeting imminent, offering diplomatic off-ramp
China has signaled willingness to buy more US products and open markets
Previous trade deals vetoed by Trump, creating trust deficit (Washington Post)
Tariff rate on $200B tranche scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019 — serves as credible threat

sources_cited.source_id: www.brookings.edu — Unpacked: The US-China Trade War
sources_cited.excerpt: The price of soybeans is already down 20 percent. This is not a big hit for the overall U.S. economy but it will hurt some specific sectors. On the whole this is a minor blip so the Trump administration will probably not change its strategy soon.

sources_cited.source_id: www.foxbusiness.com — The U.S.-China Trade War, Explained
sources_cited.excerpt: The $250 billion aggregate tariff amount that we reach after these new tariffs were put in place is about half of U.S.-China trade. If all the threats and allegations with regard to tariffs are followed through upon, all of U.S.-China trade is set to be under some kind of tariff barrier in 2018.

sources_cited.source_id: www.washingtonpost.com — How the U.S. and China misread the signals in the trade war
sources_cited.excerpt: Chinese leaders believed they had a trade agreement last year with Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, only to see President Trump veto it. In May, they reached a second deal with Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, but Trump again turned thumbs down.

sources_cited.source_id: www.brookings.edu — Unpacked: The US-China Trade War
sources_cited.excerpt: China is willing to buy more products from the U.S. and open more markets, so their offer is clear. After the 2018 elections, we're likely to see the two sides come together and negotiate something so that they can both save face.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should maintain its retaliatory posture and signal willingness to match any further U.S. tariff escalation, while privately exploring back-channel diplomatic engagement ahead of the planned Trump-Xi meeting at the G20 in Buenos Aires (Nov 30 - Dec 1). Do not preemptively concede before the G20 summit, as this would weaken China's negotiating position. Prepare a list of targeted retaliatory measures that can be deployed if the U.S. escalates further, while keeping the door open for a structured negotiation framework.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.55 reflects the significant and growing economic pressure China faces. The U.S. has already imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese imports (roughly half of all U.S.-China trade), with the September 24 round of 10% tariffs on $200 billion set to rise to 25% at year-end 2018 (Fox Business/Motley Fool transcript). President Trump has threatened to tariff the remaining $267 billion of Chinese imports if China retaliates, which would cover 100% of bilateral trade. China's retaliatory capacity is constrained — it imports only ~$130 billion of U.S. goods, meaning it cannot match U.S. tariffs dollar-for-dollar (CBS News). The Brookings analysis notes that while the overall U.S. economic impact is a 'minor blip,' specific Chinese export sectors and the broader supply chain ecosystem are under real pressure. The Washington Post reporting reveals that China has been burned repeatedly by the Trump administration — deals reached with Ross and Mnuchin were both vetoed by Trump — creating deep distrust about whether any agreement will hold.

The action score of -1.0 (retaliate) is justified because: (1) China has already retaliated with tariffs on $110 billion of $130 billion in U.S. imports, covering nearly all trade (Fox Business), so this posture is consistent with established strategy; (2) preemptive concession before the G20 summit would signal weakness and invite further demands; (3) the Trump administration views the trade war as politically beneficial for domestic purposes (Brookings), meaning concessions without reciprocal moves are unlikely to be rewarded; (4) China's offer to buy more U.S. products and open markets is already on the table (Brookings), so the negotiating position is clear. The key is to maintain leverage heading into the G20 while avoiding actions that would trigger the full $267 billion tariff threat.
key_factors: U.S. tariffs on $250B of Chinese imports, with threat to tariff remaining $267B
China's retaliatory capacity constrained by smaller import base (~$130B U.S. goods)
September 24 tariffs (10%) set to rise to 25% at end of 2018
Repeated U.S. veto of prior trade deals (Ross deal, Mnuchin deal) erodes trust
G20 summit (Nov 30 - Dec 1) offers near-term diplomatic opportunity
Trump administration views trade war as domestic political asset
China has already tariffed nearly 100% of U.S. imports it receives

sources_cited.excerpt: Effective Sept. 24, President Trump announced a 10% tariff on $200 billion in Chinese imports. That tariff is currently 10%, but at the end of 2018, that's expected to rise to 25%... The $250 billion aggregate tariff amount... is about half of U.S.-China trade
China has promised to respond in kind, but it would be unable to match that amount since it imported only $130 billion of U.S. goods last year
It is unlikely that the Chinese leadership will cave in and do anything major. China is willing to buy more products from the U.S. and open more markets, so their offer is clear
